title: Civil rights group calls for Malkus Bridge to be renamed
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
Civil rights group calls for Malkus Bridge to be renamed

 April 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1046
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In a virtual meeting Monday morning, the Caucus of African American Leaders voted to ask state officials to rename the Frederick C. Malkus Jr. Bridge, citing Malkus' "resistance to desegregation."The group, a statewide consortium of civil rights groups including the NAACP, the United Black Clergy of Maryland and others, hand-delivered a resolution with their recommendation to Gov. Wes Moore's desk later Monday, according to Carl Snowden, convener of the caucus. Snowden said the group would continue discussions on the matter in their quarterly meetings with the governor to address any future steps.
The bridge was named for Frederick C. Malkus Jr., a long-serving state legislator from near Cambridge who was instrumental in finding the funding for the bridge's ultimate construction. The structure spans the Choptank River between Talbot and Dorchester counties.
"They recommend that Senator Frederick Malkus Memorial Bridge be renamed in honor of the late Gloria Richardson, a pioneer in civil rights and a leader in the State of Maryland," read a press release sent out immediately following the vote. "The late Governor Harry R. Hughes opposed naming the bridge after Senator Malkus because of Malkus' resistance to desegregation in the 1960s and 1970s."
The caucus also passed a resolution calling for state officials to consider renaming of the Francis Scott Key Memorial Bridge, which collapsed last month after being struck by a cargo ship, resulting in the death of six construction workers who were performing late night repairs to the bridge.
"The Francis Scott Key Bridge was named in honor of a man who enslaved African Americans and wrote lyrics that scholars have indicated demeaned Black people," the Monday morning press release said.
With the 2024 General Assembly drawing to a close late Monday, Snowden said he did not anticipate any actions resulting from the caucus' resolutions until the next legislative session at the earliest.
"This may come up as early as next session. It's too late for it to happen now, but certainly in 2025 it may very well come up as an issue," he said.
When Malkus retired from the Maryland Senate in 1994, he had spent nearly five decades as a legislator.
In the 1960s, while Cambridge was going through protests against racial discrimination and Freedom Riders challenged the region's deeply rooted segregation, Malkus' civil rights voting record largely reflected the segregationist views of his mostly white, rural constituency.
The Baltimore Sun referred to him in 1966 as a "consistent opponent of civil rights legislation."
In 1962, then Gov. J. Millard Tawes called a special session of the Maryland General Assembly to consider a public accommodations law that would outlaw racial discrimination in inns, hotels, restaurants and other similar establishments.
The Eastern Shore contingent, led by Malkus, opposed the bill, and through their efforts, a provision was added to the legislation allowing counties to exempt themselves from the statute, according to Peter Levy, author of "Civil War on Race Street: The Civil Rights Movement in Cambridge, Maryland."
Levy wrote that Malkus participated in a debate on civil rights with then-Gov. of Alabama George Wallace at Goucher College in Towson, during which Malkus and Wallace denounced pending civil rights legislation as un-American.
At that debate, Malkus blamed Richardson and outsiders for the race-related troubles in Cambridge at the time, Levy said.
Richardson was best known as the leader of the Cambridge Movement, a struggle for civil rights and economic opportunities for Black people in Cambridge in the early 1960s.
In July 1963, Attorney General Robert Kennedy — who Richardson had asked earlier to provide protection for demonstrators' constitutional rights — met with Richardson, other civil rights activists and government officials to broker the Treaty of Cambridge, an agreement covering desegregation, housing and employment issues.
Snowden said past calls to rename the Malkus Bridge have drawn opposition.
"This has been controversial from day one," he said in an interview with the Star Democrat, "and it's not unusual before decisions like this are made that it's a protracted, long, sometimes intense debate on whether or not to do it."
"We're under no illusion that there won't be opposition to this, as there has been in the past," Snowden said. "The difference however is that more and more people are now becoming aware that these bridges, as well as public structures, are paid for by the taxpayers. And the question becomes, when you have a particular bridge named after someone, that person should be someone that represents all taxpayers."
Those who want to see the bridge's name preserved have, in past discussions on the matter, pointed to Malkus' role in seeing the structure built.
Later in his career, Malkus' efforts were instrumental in having the four-lane bridge that currently bears his name constructed. The bridge spanning the Choptank River replaced the deteriorating Emerson Harrington Bridge, a two-lane drawbridge constructed in the 1930s that struggled to keep up with the changing traffic needs on the Eastern Shore following the construction of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge.
For several years, Malkus introduced legislation in the General Assembly calling for the bridge's replacement. The Washington Post quoted the state senator in 1980 as saying, "This is one we're gonna win, not because they have any great love for us country boys but because the city boys will have a hell of a time getting to Ocean City without it."
Malkus introduced the bill that would ultimately lead to the bridge's construction with funding from a newly-enacted gas tax in 1985. The bridge was opened in 1987.
After the General Assembly passed legislation officially naming the bridge after Malkus, an unusual move given that Malkus was still alive at the time, then-Gov. Harry Hughes vetoed the bill.
The state legislature's override of Hughes' veto passed unanimously, according to a Washington Post article written for Malkus' retirement.
Snowden said that the caucus' call to rename the Malkus and Key bridges came in the wake of several recent efforts it has supported questioning monuments to controversial figures from history. This included the push to remove the Talbot Boys statue, a monument to Confederate soldiers, from the Talbot County Court House lawn. The efforts resulted in the statue's relocation in 2022.
"There have been five major projects similar to this which we've been successful with," Snowden said. "This is not something that focused just on the Eastern Shore. There's a national effort in the country today to begin to look at who buildings and institutions are named after."

title: Newark congregation standing strong after historic Black church is targeted with racist graffiti
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Newark congregation standing strong after historic Black church is targeted with racist graffiti

 April 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 704
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A historic Black church near Newark, Delaware, was targeted with racist graffiti and other vandalism recently, forcing the congregation to relocate its Easter services.The damage was discovered Saturday, March 30, at St. Daniel's Community Church of Iron Hill on Whittaker Road. Pastor Joseph Field said he believes it was done sometime overnight Friday into Saturday.
The vandals scrawled racial slurs all over the outside wall of the church, including the N-word, references to the KKK and the word "die." They also broke a window.
At the same time the vandalism was discovered, the church's heat stopped working, leading to fears that the outdoor propane tank had been tampered with. Field is still trying to determine exactly what happened, but as a precaution, the church canceled its Easter Sunday service and congregants instead attended service at a church in Glasgow.
"My first reaction was anger. I don't know why they would do this," Field said. "We don't bother anybody. We come here and worship and then we go home, and we're always willing to help out in the community."
The church filed a police report, and Field is hopeful the culprits are caught soon.
"We don't know who did it. We don't even know the reason why they did it now, so we can't assume too much," he said. "But as far as the racism goes, we know that's the climate in this country right now, unfortunately."
Longtime congregant Donna Johnson was the first to discover the horrifying graffiti when she arrived to clean the church on Saturday. Several generations of her family have attended St. Daniel's, and her great-grandparents are buried in the church's cemetery.
"This is not just a building," Johnson said. "This is our lives. This is our heartbeat."
St. Daniel's, which was recently listed on the National Register of Historic Places, was built in the 1850s, though there is some evidence of the congregation meeting earlier than that. Originally, it served the community of free blacks who lived in the Iron Hill area prior to the Civil War.
Today, the congregation is small, approximately 20 people, but is a tight-knit community.
"We go with what we have. Jesus only walked with 12," Field said.
Most members have longstanding family ties to the church, said Field, who has been pastor for 12 years.
"Right here, there's so much togetherness, the way they look out for one another and support one another," he added. "I love that."
Field said this is the first time St. Daniel's has been targeted, at least in recent times, but the damage done at the church this weekend appears similar to incidents that have taken place at the nearby Iron Hill Museum, which is housed in a former Black schoolhouse.
Last fall, the museum president said the property has been the victim of a sustained campaign of vandalism since January 2020. Some of the damage included racial slurs, and the worst came in March 2023 when vandals destroyed signage commemorating the legacy of Iron Hill's Black community.
Freeman Williams, president of the Newark NAACP, said the vandalism at St. Daniel's is an affront to the church's history and an attempt to denigrate and minimize the role African Americans played in the Iron Hill area.
"We're not going to let anyone's actions or activities take away from what this community is all about," Williams said. "It's strong. It's vibrant. The people here have a long legacy of strong families and pulling together. We look at this as a blip on the radar."
Williams visited the church Monday afternoon to pledge the NAACP's support.
"We're not going to stop until we find out who's responsible and we do everything in our power to make sure that person is prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law," he said.
Field said that, ultimately, the person or people behind the racist graffiti will have to answer to an even higher power.
"Because when you desecrate God's house, you're not getting in a fight with me, you're getting in a fight with God, and that's going to come back on you," he said.
Until then, he has a defiant message for anyone who thinks they can intimidate the congregation.
"We're not fearful," Field said. "We're not going anywhere. We're here to stay. We've been here this long, you're not going to chase us away."

title: 'We're serious about representing you': Department of Justice attorneys speak with community about civil rights
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'We're serious about representing you': Department of Justice attorneys speak with community about civil rights

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 582
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — At a community conversation on civil rights issues Tuesday, representatives from the U.S. Department of Justice made it clear that this conversation is the first of many."This won't be the first and last time that you see us here because we're serious about showing up," U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland Erek L. Barron said. "We're serious about representing you, hearing from you."
Community members gathered at the Harriet Tubman Center for Cultural and Educational Advancement to hear from Barron and Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Kristen Clarke and ask questions.
Clarke spoke about some of the Justice Department's highest priorities, including fighting hate crimes, holding law enforcement accountable, ensuring equal education opportunities, protecting the right to vote and combatting redlining.
Barron talked about how civil rights laws can be enforced.
"First, you've got to put your money where your mouth is," he said.
Barron said that is the reason he established the Civil Rights and Special Victims Section of the District of Maryland U.S. Attorney's Office.
He said that for civil rights laws to be enforced, the department needs to show up and establish a partnership with the community.
"That's why we're here," he said.
Clarke said there was more she could speak about regarding the efforts of the department.
"But we want to hear from you today," she said. "The purpose of this convening is to make sure that we are hearing from and learning from people in this community to ensure that the resources of the Justice Department are put to work to address the most complex and challenging problems that you face here in this community."
During the discussion, the Rev. James Jones, convener of the Caucus of African American Leaders on the Eastern Shore, said that people of color receive lengthier and more serious sentences locally and nationwide.
Barron said he is attuned to this issue. He said that last year it was pointed out to him that the U.S. Attorney's Office doesn't seem to be prosecuting as many people.
"I said, 'That's correct because we can do it smartly,'" Barron said. "'We can enforce the laws and make our state, make our cities safer without just locking everyone up if we do it with policies that are efficient and smart.'"
Lareese Cathey-Jackson, founder of the nonprofit Angels At A Distance — a prevention program for local youth — asked how programs like hers can get more funding and resources.
Clarke said that last week, the attorney general announced several new initiatives that would bring support to different communities in the nation.
"We're happy to help facilitate and make those connections," Clarke said.
After the conversation, Cathey-Jackson said these conversations need to continue and need to be consistent. She said she has been to meetings like this before where those statements just seemed like talk, but she has hope that this one is different.
"I don't feel like that coming into this meeting," she said. "I really do feel like they want to move forward."
Alex Green, co-owner of the Harriet Tubman Center for Cultural and Educational Advancement, said it was an honor to host the event in partnership with the Civil Rights Division and the Maryland U.S. Attorney's Office. He said it was great to bring people together for a conversation.
"I think it's really essential in today's climate that we have conversations about the things we don't understand," he said. "Because if we don't talk about them, ... We stay in our own little box, and we never come to a consensus or agreement on what we don't understand."

title: Historic Sotterley holds lecture on 60th anniversary of Civil Rights Act
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Historic Sotterley holds lecture on 60th anniversary of Civil Rights Act

 April 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 713
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's been 60 years since the Civil Rights Act was enacted in 1964 and a panel of experts came together April 10 to discuss "How far have we come, and where do we need to go?"The virtual discussion was the second in Historic Sotterley's Presents People and Places series.
The lecture comprised of moderator and St. Mary's College Community Affairs Liaison Kelsey R.M. Bush, Starr Center for the Study of the American at Washington College Deputy Director Jaelon T. Moaney, St. Mary's College of Maryland senior Phoebe Tate and Roderick Lewis, who is Sen. Ben Cardin's Southern Maryland field representative.
"They are incredible leaders who are starting to move forward in this world," Historic Sotterley Executive Director Nancy Easterling said of the panel, "and making a real difference, and their ideas and perspectives will be appreciated."
A news release stated the Civil Rights Act was a milestone in American democracy and justice, dismantling Jim Crow laws and paving a way for racial and gender equality. But with all the progress made, equality is still something that eludes many in the nation.
"Sixty years might seem like a long time ago for some of us," Bush said. "But as they say, 'Time and even age are relative.' To put it into perspective, in our world today there is an affinity to denigrate young voices because of their lack of experience or they need to show respect. However, we forget that many of the voices that led to the Civil Rights Movement belonged to young people, especially for them to say, 'Enough.' Young people have been leaders and voices of change, and over time were proven that they were correct."
The panel discussed how they view the progress that has been made in the previous 60 years, and the challenges that they feel we still see face today.
"One of the greatest achievements of the Civil Rights Movement is the ability for people of diverse backgrounds to actually come together and actually have the opportunity to interact with one another," Tate said. "It also gives many voices that have been marginalized and disenfranchised for much of the history of this country to have that opportunity to join in."
Bush asked how the Civil Rights Act of 1964 impacted the panelists' lives and those around them.
"I see it as a guarantee that I am valued pretty much in the workplace," said Tate, who interned at Historic Sotterley last year and is working on a St. Mary's Project adapting slave narratives into a graphic novel. "And no matter what, I cannot be discriminated against, and if this does happen I have the backings of the legality and the government that this cannot stand."
"I immediately think to what type of opportunities my grandparents, my parents would have had if it wasn't for the Civil Rights Amendment, let alone the opportunities my siblings and I would have been able to have," said Lewis, who is a graduate of St. Mary's College of Maryland and a member of the St. Mary's NAACP. "It really opened up society in many ways for Black Americans to have access to spaces that they were not allowed to be in before, so it was a major achievement in the struggle to advance civil rights in this country. It's really hard to think how life would be without it."
Bush welcomed Moaney to the conversation, whose appearance had been delayed by computer issues.
"Much like the theme for tonight's conversation is 'We Prevail,' I'm grateful to have gotten over those technical difficulties," said Moaney, who is a descendant of founding Black families in Kent and Talbot counties, and who was appointed by Gov. Wes Moore to the Maryland Commission on African American History & Culture.
Bush asked the panelists what challenges still exist in achieving true equity for all regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation or identities.
"We need to be very cautious about who we're speaking on behalf and for," Moaney said. "I think there are so many well-intentioned people, eager people intent on joining those on the side of equality, but it is dangerous territory to be paraphrasing and even to the extent of appropriating. We still stand to benefit from hearing so many more voices, and I don't want us to leave this call thinking that solely precluded to those being elected."
